questions.question: How do you implement a custom UserDetailsService and UserDetails in Spring Security?
questions.title: UserDetailsService and UserDetails — Custom Implementation
questions.direct_answer: **`UserDetailsService`** is a single-method interface that loads user data by username; Spring Security calls it during authentication. **`UserDetails`** is an interface describing the loaded user — credentials, four account-status flags, and granted authorities. You implement both to connect Spring Security to your own database or user store, replacing the default in-memory user management. **`DaoAuthenticationProvider`** invokes `loadUserByUsername()`, then verifies the submitted password with `PasswordEncoder`. Map status flags to real columns (locked, enabled, password-expired) so flipping a flag in the DB instantly blocks login without code changes.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate can wire Spring Security to a real user database — the most common integration task.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Returning a plain Spring Security User object without implementing account expiry or lock flags, causing confusing authentication failures.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss caching UserDetails to avoid database hits on every request, UserDetailsPasswordService for password upgrade, and the difference between isEnabled() and isAccountNonLocked().

sections.title: UserDetailsService Bridges Your Database to Spring Security's Auth Engine
sections.content:
Spring Security doesn't care where users live — RDBMS, LDAP, REST API, or an in-memory map. It only needs a **`UserDetailsService`** that takes a username and returns a **`UserDetails`** object. Your entire user model is funneled through this one-method interface.

The `UserDetails` contract carries everything Spring needs: **username**, **hashed password**, **four account-status booleans**, and a collection of **`GrantedAuthority`** objects. **`DaoAuthenticationProvider`** calls `loadUserByUsername()`, receives the result, and then uses **`PasswordEncoder`** to verify the submitted password against the stored hash.

The separation is intentional: Spring Security's engine never sees your `User` entity directly — only `UserDetails`.
- This lets you evolve the domain model without breaking authentication.
- The common mistake is hardcoding the four status booleans to `true` and only adding lockout logic later — by then the column exists but the flag does nothing.
- **Map every flag to a real entity field from day one**.

sections.title: Authentication Flow: Filter -> Manager -> Provider -> UserDetailsService
sections.content:
```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Client
    participant Filter as "UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter"
    participant Manager as "AuthenticationManager (ProviderManager)"
    participant Provider as "DaoAuthenticationProvider"
    participant Uds as "UserDetailsService"
    participant Encoder as "PasswordEncoder"
    participant Holder as "SecurityContextHolder"
    Client->>Filter: "POST /login (username + password)"
    Filter->>Filter: "build UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken (unauthenticated)"
    Filter->>Manager: "authenticate(token)"
    Manager->>Provider: "delegate to supports(UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken)"
    Provider->>Uds: "loadUserByUsername(username)"
    Uds-->>Provider: "UserDetails (hash + authorities + status flags)"
    Provider->>Provider: "check status flags (enabled, nonLocked, etc)"
    Provider->>Encoder: "matches(rawPassword, storedHash)"
    Encoder-->>Provider: "true / false"
    Provider-->>Manager: "authenticated token (with authorities)"
    Manager-->>Filter: "authenticated Authentication"
    Filter->>Holder: "setContext(SecurityContext with auth)"
    Filter-->>Client: "302 redirect to success URL + session cookie"
```

sections.title: The Four Status Flags That Cause Silent Auth Failures
Wiring loadUserByUsername and the ROLE_ Prefix
Caching UserDetails and UserDetailsPasswordService
sections.content:
**When caching matters:**
- Session-based: `loadUserByUsername()` runs once per login, then session holds the principal
- Stateless JWT: only at token issue — subsequent requests don't touch the DB
- Per-request DB hit only if you re-load the user to recheck roles every call

**`@Cacheable` on the loader:**

```java
@Cacheable(value = "userDetails", key = "#username")
@Override
public UserDetails loadUserByUsername(String username) {
    return userRepo.findByEmail(username)
        .map(AppUserDetails::new)
        .orElseThrow(() -> new UsernameNotFoundException(username));
}
```

**Cache hygiene:**
- TTL of 1-5 minutes is the sweet spot
- Evict on user updates: `@CacheEvict(value = "userDetails", key = "#user.email")`
- For multi-instance deployments use Redis-backed cache, not in-memory

**`UserDetailsPasswordService` — transparent algorithm upgrade:**
- On successful login, `DelegatingPasswordEncoder` detects the stored hash uses an outdated algorithm (e.g., BCrypt cost 10 when you've moved to Argon2)
- Spring calls `updatePassword(UserDetails, newPasswordHash)`
- You persist the new hash; users migrate lazily on login — no bulk migration, no reset
- Implement on the same class as `UserDetailsService` and Spring auto-wires it

sections.title: Custom UserDetails: When It Helps and What to Watch
sections.content:
**When it helps:**
- Your authorization expressions need custom claims (tenant ID, subscription tier, feature flags)
- You want lazy password algorithm upgrade via `UserDetailsPasswordService`
- You need to expose account-state flags (locked, expired) to admin UIs without re-querying
- You map IdP attributes (groups, departments) to authorities

**When it hurts:**
- For trivial apps the default `User.builder()` is enough — custom impl is overkill
- Embedding heavyweight entities (full `User` JPA entity with collections) in the principal causes `LazyInitializationException` after the session closes
- Unbounded role list per user blows up session size; cap or paginate

**Watch for:**
- **Username enumeration** — return identical error for unknown user vs wrong password
- **PII in logs** — never `toString()` the principal in logs without redaction
- **Stale cache** — evict on role/status change or admin actions become invisible
- **`equals`/`hashCode`** — needed if `UserDetails` instances are used as map keys (rare)
- **Serialization** — `UserDetails` must be `Serializable` for HTTP session replication or Spring Session

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`UserDetailsService.loadUserByUsername()`** is the bridge between your DB and Spring Security — single method, returns `UserDetails`.
- **Four status flags** (`isEnabled`, `isAccountNonLocked`, `isAccountNonExpired`, `isCredentialsNonExpired`) each block login with a distinct exception; map them to real entity columns.
- **`ROLE_` prefix** is required when using `hasRole()`; omit it and authorization silently fails.
- **`UsernameNotFoundException` should not leak user existence** — let `DaoAuthenticationProvider` convert to generic `"Bad credentials"`.
- **`UserDetailsPasswordService`** enables transparent password rehashing on login (BCrypt -> Argon2) with no user disruption.
- **Cache `UserDetails` with `@Cacheable`** for session-based apps where the user is reloaded frequently; evict on role/status changes.
- **`DaoAuthenticationProvider` is replaceable** — implement `AuthenticationProvider` for OAuth2 tokens, LDAP, SAML, or API keys; `ProviderManager` tries them in order.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**Bridge contract**
- `UserDetailsService` has one method: `loadUserByUsername(String)` returning `UserDetails`
- Connects Spring Security to any user store (DB, LDAP, REST)
- `DaoAuthenticationProvider` calls it during authentication, then uses `PasswordEncoder.matches`

**Implementation pattern**
- Implement `UserDetailsService` as a `@Service` bean — Spring Boot auto-wires it
- Implement `UserDetails` on a wrapper around your `AppUser` entity
- Map `getAuthorities()` from your roles, prefixing with `ROLE_`

**Status flag pitfalls**
- Four booleans: enabled, account-non-expired, account-non-locked, credentials-non-expired
- Each maps to a different exception (Disabled, Expired, Locked, CredentialsExpired)
- All converted to generic `"Bad credentials"` to prevent enumeration
- Map them to real columns so admin actions take effect immediately

**Performance**
- Per-request DB hit only matters with session-based + reload-every-request pattern
- Cache with `@Cacheable`, TTL 1-5 min, evict on user updates
- For Spring Session/Redis, principal is in the session — no per-request lookup

**Algorithm migration**
- Implement `UserDetailsPasswordService.updatePassword`
- `DelegatingPasswordEncoder` detects old algorithm and re-hashes with new one on login
- Persist the new hash — lazy migration with zero user impact

**Security**
- Same error message for unknown user and wrong password
- Never log password or full principal
- Use opaque session IDs; rotate on login (prevents fixation)

questions.question: What are the trade-offs between session-based and token-based authentication in Spring Security?
questions.title: Session-Based vs Token-Based Authentication
questions.direct_answer: **Session-based** authentication stores user state server-side, tied to a cookie — instant revocation, but needs sticky sessions or a shared store (Redis) in clusters. **Token-based** (typically JWT) is stateless: all data is encoded in the token, scaling horizontally with no shared state, but **revocation is hard until the token expires**. Sessions are simpler and correct for monolithic web apps; **JWTs are right for APIs and microservices** where each service independently validates tokens. Opaque tokens with introspection are the middle ground when you need stateless transport plus instant revocation.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands stateful vs stateless architecture trade-offs, not just syntax.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Claiming JWTs are always better — missing that revocation, token size, and secret management are real drawbacks.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss opaque tokens with an introspection endpoint as a middle ground, or refresh token rotation as a revocation strategy.

sections.title: Stateful vs Stateless: The Revocation Trade-off
sections.content:
Developers default to JWT because **"stateless is better."** The missing nuance: stateless means the server **cannot invalidate a token until it expires**.
- If an account is compromised you cannot force logout — the JWT is valid for hours or days.
- Add a blocklist to fix this and you've reintroduced server-side state, often building a worse session system.

**Session-based** stores only a 32-byte session ID in the cookie. The server (or shared Redis) holds the data. `session.invalidate()` instantly renders the ID useless. The trade-off is **coordination in clusters** — sticky sessions or a shared store add complexity and latency.

**Token-based** (JWT) embeds claims in the token sent on every request. The server validates the signature without storage. **JWT downsides interviewers test:** size (~800+ bytes vs 32), payload is **encoded, not encrypted** (anyone with the token reads claims), and revocation requires a blocklist.

sections.title: Sessions vs JWTs: Every Trade-off That Matters
sections.content:
Neither approach is universally correct. Pick by architecture, not fashion.

| Aspect | Session-Based | Token-Based (JWT) |
|---|---|---|
| **State location** | Server-side (memory or Redis) | Client-side (inside the token) |
| **Scaling** | Sticky sessions or shared store | Stateless — any server validates |
| **Revocation** | Instant — `session.invalidate()` | Not possible without a blocklist |
| **Token size** | 32-byte session ID cookie | 800+ bytes per request |
| **XSS risk** | Low — `HttpOnly` + `Secure` cookie | High if stored in `localStorage` |
| **CSRF risk** | Yes — cookies sent automatically | No — `Authorization` header requires JS |
| **Cross-domain** | Cookie domain restrictions | Easy — `Authorization` header anywhere |
| **Best for** | Web apps, admin panels, monoliths | APIs, microservices, mobile clients |
| **Spring config** | `SessionCreationPolicy.IF_REQUIRED` | `SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS` |

**Watch:** if you store a JWT in a cookie you gain `HttpOnly` but **reintroduce CSRF** — re-enable Spring's CSRF protection. Expired tokens produce **401**, not 403, even if the user is active — surprises devs who used long-lived dev tokens.

sections.title: Opaque Tokens and Refresh Rotation: The Middle Ground
sections.content:
**Opaque tokens — random strings with no embedded claims:**
- Look like session IDs to the client
- Resource servers introspect them at the auth server's `/introspect` endpoint
- Auth server returns claims; revoking is one DB row update
- Caching introspection 30-60s reduces load while keeping near-real-time revocation
- Pattern used by Stripe, Twilio, GitHub PATs
- Cost: extra hop per request unless cached

**Refresh token rotation — practical revocation in JWT model:**
- Access tokens expire in 15-30 minutes (small theft window)
- Refresh tokens are longer-lived but **rotate on each use** (new refresh token issued every time)
- If an attacker uses a stolen refresh token, the legitimate user's next refresh fails — server detects reuse and revokes the family
- Automatic compromise detection without a global blocklist

**Recommendation matrix:**
- **Web app + DB monolith** -> sessions (server control, simpler CSRF/XSS story)
- **Public API / microservices** -> JWT with short expiry + refresh rotation
- **OAuth2 authorization server with revocation needs** -> opaque tokens + introspection
- **Mobile clients** -> JWT (no cookie semantics) + refresh rotation
- **Hybrid (BFF pattern)** -> session cookie at the edge, JWT propagated to backend services

sections.title: When Sessions Help, When JWTs Help, What to Watch
sections.content:
**When sessions help:**
- Monolithic web app with a single DB or Redis
- Need instant logout for compliance (banking, healthcare)
- Server-rendered MVC where cookies are natural
- Want minimal request payload

**When JWTs help:**
- Microservices where every service must validate independently
- Mobile/SPA clients where cookies are awkward
- Cross-domain APIs (no cookie domain pain)
- Need offline / no-DB validation at the edge (CDN, API gateway)

**When it hurts:**
- JWT for an app that must instantly revoke -> you build a blocklist anyway
- Sessions across many regions without cluster-wide Redis -> sticky sessions break under failover
- Putting PII in JWT claims -> data exposure (payload is base64, not encrypted)
- Long-lived JWTs (24h+) without refresh -> theft window is huge

**Watch for:**
- **Token size** in headers — proxies often cap header size at 8KB; bloated JWTs break
- **Clock skew** — JWT `exp` rejects with even a few seconds of drift; allow tolerance
- **Key rotation** — `JwkSet` URL with multiple keys is the answer; never hardcode one key
- **Logout UX** — session-based logout is real; JWT logout is client-side only without a blocklist
- **`SameSite=Lax` defaults** — modern browsers may break cross-site session cookies

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Sessions = server-side state; JWT = client-side state** — sessions need shared storage in clusters; JWT is self-contained.
- **JWT cannot be revoked before expiry** without a blocklist; a stolen JWT is valid until `exp`.
- **JWT payload is base64-encoded, not encrypted** — never put PII or secrets in claims.
- **Opaque tokens + introspection** give stateless transport with instant revocation — the pragmatic middle ground.
- **Refresh token rotation** detects token theft automatically by invalidating the family on reuse.
- **`SameSite=Strict` cookies** prevent CSRF without tokens — modern browser default makes session-based safer than ever.
- **Pick by architecture, not trend** — monolith web -> session; microservice API -> JWT; OAuth2 server -> opaque + introspect.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**Two models, opposite trade-offs**
- Session-based: server-side state, instant revocation, needs shared store in clusters
- JWT-based: stateless, scales horizontally, revocation hard until expiry

**Session-based flow**
- Login -> server creates session, stores in memory or Redis -> client gets session cookie
- Each request: server looks up session ID -> authenticated
- Logout: `session.invalidate()` — instant
- Sticky sessions OR shared Redis required across instances

**JWT-based flow**
- Login -> server signs JWT with claims -> client stores it, sends in `Authorization: Bearer`
- Each request: server verifies signature — no DB lookup
- Revocation: build a Redis blocklist of revoked JTIs (now you have state)
- Refresh tokens with rotation give automatic theft detection

**JWT payload is not secret**
- Base64-decoded reveals everything
- Signed != encrypted
- Don't put passwords, PII, or secrets in claims
- Use a separate `/me` endpoint for sensitive data

**Opaque tokens — middle ground**
- Random string, no embedded claims
- Stored in the auth server (Redis); each request introspects
- Revocable instantly, one Redis lookup per request
- Cache introspection 30-60s for performance

**The architectural rule**
- Web monolith with DB -> sessions, simpler
- API or microservice -> JWT, stateless
- OAuth2 server with revocation -> opaque + introspect
- Don't pick JWT just because it's trendy

questions.question: How should passwords be stored, and what are the differences between BCrypt and Argon2?
questions.title: Password Hashing — BCrypt vs Argon2
questions.direct_answer: Passwords must never be stored in plaintext or reversibly encrypted — only **one-way adaptive hashing** functions designed for passwords. **BCrypt** (1999) is the widely-deployed standard with a configurable cost factor. **Argon2id** is the 2015 PHC winner, OWASP-recommended, with **memory-hardness** that makes GPU attacks economically impractical. Spring Security's **`PasswordEncoder`** abstraction supports both via **`DelegatingPasswordEncoder`**, which prefixes hashes with the algorithm (`{bcrypt}...`, `{argon2}...`) and enables transparent migration on next login.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands why general-purpose hash functions (MD5, SHA-256) are inappropriate for passwords and what makes a password hashing function secure.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Suggesting SHA-256 with a salt as sufficient for password storage — it is orders of magnitude faster than BCrypt and vulnerable to GPU attacks.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the importance of cost factor tuning to target ~100ms hash time, how DelegatingPasswordEncoder handles algorithm migration, and the risk of pepper vs salt.

sections.title: Why Fast Hashes (SHA-256, MD5) Are Wrong for Passwords
sections.content:
The fundamental problem with **SHA-256, MD5**, or any general-purpose hash for password storage is **speed**.
- SHA-256 was designed to be as fast as possible — a modern GPU computes **~10 billion** SHA-256 hashes per second.
- An attacker with a stolen DB tests billions of guesses per second.
- Salting prevents rainbow-table lookups but **doesn't slow brute force at all** — the attacker hashes salt+guess at full GPU speed.

**Password hashing functions are intentionally slow.** **BCrypt**, **Argon2**, and **scrypt** consume configurable time and memory per hash. BCrypt at the right cost takes **~100ms** — a billion times slower than SHA-256. Offline brute force becomes impractically expensive even with stolen hashes.

Spring's **`DelegatingPasswordEncoder`** solves the migration problem: it embeds the algorithm in the hash string (`{bcrypt}$2a$...`, `{argon2}$argon2id$...`).
- The app accepts multiple algorithms simultaneously.
- With **`UserDetailsPasswordService`**, a user logging in with an old BCrypt hash is **lazily re-hashed** with Argon2 on success — no bulk migration, no forced reset.

sections.title: BCrypt vs Argon2id: Speed, Memory-Hardness, GPU Resistance
sections.content:
Argon2's edge over BCrypt is **memory-hardness** — GPUs can't parallelize memory-intensive ops the way they parallelize compute.

| Aspect | BCrypt | Argon2id |
|---|---|---|
| **Year** | 1999 | 2015 (PHC winner) |
| **Cost dimensions** | Time only (work factor, 2^N iterations) | Time + Memory + Parallelism |
| **Memory hardness** | None | Yes — configurable RAM per hash |
| **GPU resistance** | Moderate | High — bound by RAM bandwidth |
| **Password length** | Max 72 bytes (silent truncation) | No practical limit |
| **Spring class** | `BCryptPasswordEncoder` (default) | `Argon2PasswordEncoder` |
| **NIST SP 800-63B** | Acceptable | Preferred |
| **Encoding prefix** | `{bcrypt}` | `{argon2}` |

**BCrypt's 72-byte limit** is subtle: passwords > 72 chars are silently truncated. Two different long passwords can hash identically. For passphrases, use Argon2 or pre-hash with SHA-256 before BCrypt.

**Argon2id memory cost** (recommended 64MB+) is what beats GPUs: each parallel attempt needs 64MB; aggregate RAM bandwidth becomes the bottleneck instead of compute throughput. Ten GPUs give ten times compute but can't beat the memory wall.

sections.title: Cost Factor Tuning and Lazy Migration
When to Upgrade and How to Migrate Existing Hashes
sections.content:
**BCrypt's structural limit:**
- Cost factor scales **time** only, not memory
- GPU crackers parallelize across thousands of cores
- Modern GPUs crack BCrypt cost-10 in milliseconds per guess in a distributed setup

**Argon2 advantage:**
- **Memory parameter** makes GPU cracking economically impractical
- Argon2id (recommended variant) needs gigabytes of RAM to scale across millions of parallel threads
- Three knobs: `memory` (RAM amount), `iterations` (time cost), `parallelism` (concurrent lanes)

**Spring support:**
- BCrypt: `new BCryptPasswordEncoder(12)`
- Argon2: `Argon2PasswordEncoder.defaultsForSpringSecurity_v5_8()`
- Both compatible with `DelegatingPasswordEncoder` algorithm prefixes

**Migration without forcing re-entry:**
- On login, validate against stored hash with current algorithm
- If old algorithm detected, re-hash with new algorithm and update DB
- User experiences nothing different
- After migration completes (most users have logged in), disable old algorithm in the encoder map

**Practical guidance:**
- BCrypt cost 12-14 remains acceptable in 2026
- Argon2 is a depth improvement, not an emergency vulnerability fix
- Prioritize Argon2 for new apps; planned migration for existing ones

sections.title: Salt vs Pepper, and What to Watch
sections.content:
**When BCrypt helps:**
- Mature library coverage in every language and framework
- Battle-tested for 25 years
- Simple to tune (one knob: cost)
- Adequate for most B2B/SaaS apps

**When Argon2id helps:**
- High-value targets (fintech, healthcare, government)
- Threat model includes well-funded attackers with GPU farms
- Allowing passphrases > 72 chars
- Compliance requires PHC-winner / NIST-preferred algorithm

**Watch for:**
- **Salt vs pepper**
  - Salt: per-password random value stored alongside hash; built into BCrypt/Argon2 automatically
  - Pepper: app-wide secret added to password before hashing; stored outside DB (KMS/HSM)
  - Pepper helps if DB leaks but app secrets don't; rotation is hard (need to track which pepper)
- **Cost factor too low** -> brute-forceable
- **Cost factor too high** -> login takes seconds, DOS surface
- **No `PasswordEncoder` bean** -> Spring Boot fails on startup (since 5.7+)
- **Calling `encoder.encode()` at every comparison** instead of `encoder.matches()` — never compare hashes manually
- **MD5/SHA-1 still in legacy systems** — wrap with `NoOpPasswordEncoder` only for read-only compatibility, then migrate

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Never use MD5, SHA-1, SHA-256 for passwords** — they're fast by design; GPU computes 10B+/sec.
- **BCrypt cost 10-12 is the current baseline; tune to ~100ms** — `new BCryptPasswordEncoder(12)`; +1 doubles time.
- **Argon2id is OWASP-recommended (2023+)** — resists GPU and side-channel attacks via memory-hardness.
- **`DelegatingPasswordEncoder` enables algorithm migration** — `{bcrypt}hash` / `{argon2}hash` prefixes; current algorithm for new passwords; old verified by their algorithm.
- **`UserDetailsPasswordService.updatePassword`** lazily upgrades hashes on login — no forced reset.
- **`PasswordEncoderFactories.createDelegatingPasswordEncoder()`** is the Spring Boot default — always use a bean.
- **BCrypt's 72-byte truncation** is a subtle bug for passphrases — use Argon2 or pre-hash with SHA-256.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**Why fast hashes fail for passwords**
- SHA-256: ~10B hashes/sec on a consumer GPU
- 8-char password: ~200T combinations — crackable in hours with dictionary attacks
- BCrypt cost 12: ~100ms/hash -> 10/sec/GPU -> decades for the same space

**BCrypt**
- Configurable work factor: `new BCryptPasswordEncoder(12)`
- Each +1 doubles compute time; tune to ~100ms
- Random salt automatic — no two BCrypt hashes of the same password match
- 72-byte limit; truncation is silent

**Argon2id — modern choice**
- 2015 Password Hashing Competition winner
- OWASP recommendation (2023+)
- Memory-hard — beats GPU farms
- Three params: memory (64MB+), iterations (3), parallelism (2)
- `Argon2PasswordEncoder.defaultsForSpringSecurity_v5_8()`

**Migration without breaking logins**
- `DelegatingPasswordEncoder` prefixes hashes: `{bcrypt}$2a$12$...` or `{argon2}$argon2id$...`
- Old BCrypt hashes verify correctly; new passwords use current default
- Implement `UserDetailsPasswordService.updatePassword` for transparent re-hashing on login
- After migration, disable old algorithm in the encoder map

**Operational rules**
- Always inject `PasswordEncoder` as a bean — never compare hashes manually
- Use `encoder.matches(raw, hash)`; never re-encode for comparison
- Salt is automatic; pepper (app-wide secret) is optional defense-in-depth
- Revisit cost factors yearly as hardware improves

**Recommendation for 2026**
- New apps: Argon2id default, BCrypt fallback
- Existing apps: keep BCrypt cost 12+, plan transparent migration to Argon2
